newsitem.title: UK: Britain warns "Loyalists" after N.Irish bombings.
newsitem.headline: Britain warns "Loyalists" after N.Irish bombings.

text.p: Britain warned on Tuesday that a spate of bombings by pro-British "Loyalist" guerrillas could lead to their political allies being expelled from Northern Ireland peace talks.

A spate of bomb attacks by guerrillas of the Irish Republican Army, to which the Loyalists have responded with bombings of their own, has put the shaky Northern Ireland peace process under increasing strain.

The latest Loyalist incidents "inevitably raise questions over the position in the Northern Ireland talks of the two parties associated with the Loyalist paramilitaries," the Northern Ireland Office said in a statement.

"The government shares the increasing public concern that has arisen as a result of recent car bomb attacks, the first two of which have been attributed by the (police) Chief Constable to Loyalist extremists," it said.

The warning coincided with rising tension in the British province where security has been tightened to combat a series of attacks by resurgent Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas and retaliatory strikes by Loyalist extremists.

Two Loyalist parties, the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP) and the Ulster Democratic Party (UDP), are allowed to take part in current multi-party talks because the Loyalists' commanders have operated a truce since October 1994.

But the truce has frayed under pressure of a fresh surge in IRA hostilities and last week the province's police chief confirmed publicly his suspicions that Loyalist foot-soldiers were behind two booby trap attacks on Catholics.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew said last week that he believed that despite the incidents, the loyalist commanders in the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), had not abandonded their truce.

The government statement on Tuesday said that other parties in the talks would have an opportunity next Monday to question the continued presence of Loyalists politicians when a plenary session is chaired by former U.S.senator George Mitchell.

"It is open to to any participant under the talks' rules of procedure to make a representation that a participant is no longer entitled to be at the talks, for having demonstrably dishonoured the Mitchell Principles of democracy and non- violence," the statement said.

Mainstream parties supported by pro-British Protestants say that the Loyalist politicians should be expelled -- but sources in many of the other parties say expulsion would be a blow to whatever influence they wield with the Loyalist hardliners.
Loyalist parties insist the CLMC truce is still intact and will remain so until the CLMC declares otherwise.
Sinn Fein, the IRA's political arm, is barred from the talks because the republican guerrillas refuse to call a truce.
